name: Horner nested polynomial evaluation
definition: For P(x)=Σ_(j=0)^d a_j x^j, set b_d=a_d and b_j=a_j+x b_(j+1) for j=d−1,…,0; P(x)=b_0.
variables: d nonnegative degree; a_j coefficients; x scalar argument
assumptions: Finite scalar coefficients and argument in a commutative field; standard monomial basis
limitations: Cancellation and overflow can affect floating-point results; not a stable relative-error guarantee near roots
computation: Evaluate descending coefficients using d multiplications and d additions in exact arithmetic; d=0 returns the constant. Use finite-precision safeguards where appropriate.

source.citation: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions §1.11(i), equations 1.11.1–1.11.4. https://dlmf.nist.gov/1.11.i

application: General polynomial evaluation; no forecasting benefit claimed.
mechanism_note: Induction gives b_j=Σ_(k=j)^d a_k x^(k−j), so b_0=P(x). This one-state monomial recurrence is not barycentric interpolation, a root solver, or a Chebyshev iterative linear-system solver.

name: Clenshaw Chebyshev series evaluation
variables: T_j first-kind Chebyshev polynomial; a_j full series coefficients; d nonnegative degree; x real argument
assumptions: Finite expansion with full constant coefficient and x in [−1,1]
limitations: Roundoff and cancellation remain possible, especially near endpoints; extrapolation may amplify error
computation: Backward two-state recurrence in O(d) arithmetic and O(1) auxiliary storage; d=0 returns a_0.

source.citation: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions §3.11(ii), equations 3.11.11 and 3.11.15. https://dlmf.nist.gov/3.11.ii

application: General Chebyshev expansion evaluation; no forecasting benefit claimed.
incompatible_methods: Coefficients in unrelated basis without conversion
mechanism_note: The DLMF uses half-weighted c_0; set c_0=2a_0 and c_j=a_j for j>0. Substitution into its final (u_0−u_2)/2 gives the stated full-coefficient formula. This two-state recurrence is a generalization of Horner but uses a materially different recurrence for an orthogonal basis; neither Clenshaw–Curtis quadrature nor Chebyshev iteration evaluates this supplied expansion.

name: De Casteljau Bernstein polynomial evaluation
definition: For P(t)=Σ_(i=0)^d β_i C(d,i)t^i(1−t)^(d−i), set b_i^(0)=β_i and b_i^(r)=(1−t)b_i^(r−1)+t b_(i+1)^(r−1) for r=1,…,d and i=0,…,d−r; P(t)=b_0^(d).
variables: d nonnegative degree; C(d,i) binomial coefficient; β_i real Bernstein coefficients; t scalar argument; b intermediate values
assumptions: Finite scalar Bernstein coefficients and t in [0,1]; exact arithmetic for the identity
limitations: Quadratic arithmetic cost; cancellation may still matter for mixed-sign coefficients; extrapolation loses convex combination property
failure_conditions: Coefficients supplied in a different basis
Invalid parameter interval for the bounded specification
In-place recurrence overwritten in the wrong order
computation: Initialize a length d+1 array with coefficients; update increasing i at each level using the preceding level values. Uses d(d+1)/2 linear blends and O(d) auxiliary space; d=0 returns β_0.

source.citation: Eric W. Weisstein, MathWorld, de Casteljau Algorithm, equations (1)–(3). https://mathworld.wolfram.com/deCasteljauAlgorithm.html

application: General Bernstein polynomial evaluation; no forecasting benefit claimed.
required_inputs: Bernstein coefficients and scalar t in [0,1]
incompatible_methods: Treating monomial coefficients as Bernstein coefficients
mechanism_note: Induction using Pascal's identity yields b_i^(r)=Σ_(j=0)^r C(r,j)t^j(1−t)^(r−j)β_(i+j). Each level is a triangular array of convex combinations, distinct from the scalar backward Horner or Clenshaw recurrence.

name: Newton divided difference polynomial interpolation
definition: For distinct nodes x_0,…,x_d and ordinates y_i set D_(i,0)=y_i; D_(i,r)=(D_(i+1,r−1)−D_(i,r−1))/(x_(i+r)−x_i) for r=1,…,d and i=0,…,d−r. P(x)=Σ_(r=0)^d D_(0,r) Π_(j=0)^(r−1)(x−x_j), with empty product 1.
variables: d nonnegative degree bound; x_i distinct nodes; y_i ordinates; D divided differences; x query
assumptions: Finite distinct real nodes, finite ordinates and scalar query; no repeated-node derivative data
limitations: Same polynomial and possible high-degree oscillation as barycentric interpolation; close nodes can amplify rounding; order affects finite-precision results
failure_conditions: Arithmetic overflow or nonfinite divided differences
computation: Build divided differences in O(d²) arithmetic, then evaluate nested Newton products in O(d) arithmetic. For fixed coefficients a new node extends the polynomial with one additional basis term after its divided difference is computed.

source.citation: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions §3.3(iii)–(iv), equations 3.3.34–3.3.38. https://dlmf.nist.gov/3.3

application: General interpolation of finite numerical tables; no forecasting benefit claimed.
required_inputs: Distinct nodes, associated ordinates, query point
incompatible_methods: Repeated nodes without Hermite divided-difference rules
mechanism_note: The Newton form is the same unique degree-at-most-d interpolant as the barycentric form, but uses a divided-difference table and nested product basis, allowing incremental addition of a node. Conservatively classified as a computational variant, not a new interpolant or independent algorithm count.
